Sitting there with my coffee, watching folks tend their plots, I feel two things at once: a warmth for anyone who shows up and pitches in, and a need for some simple ground rules so everyone’s comfortable.

I’m a “live and let live” guy. I don’t care where you’re from, what language you speak, who you love, or which church you go to—if you say hello, mind your manners, and treat others decently, you’re a neighbor in my book. The garden is good that way: dirt doesn’t care about our differences. Swapping tomatoes, sharing a hose, helping lift a heavy bag—those little acts break the ice faster than speeches.

Now, some situations take a steadier hand. If someone’s struggling with alcohol or drugs, I try to be respectful and not make it a spectacle. Offer help when the moment’s right—point them to local resources, make sure they know folks will watch out without judging—but also keep clear boundaries, especially with kids around. Safety first, kindness always. Same with health issues: follow the guidance, don’t pry, don’t gossip, and remember people are more than whatever they’re dealing with.

With cultural and language differences, I keep it simple: a smile, a “howdy,” learn a name, maybe a couple words in their language. Food is a bridge—bring a plate, accept a plate—and you’re halfway to friendship. I appreciate when folks share their traditions but also respect the shared rhythms of the block: reasonable noise, clean common areas, pick up after yourself, handle disagreements face to face before calling in authorities.

If there’s tension, I like starting with a conversation: “Hey, is there a better time for the music?” or “Could we keep the path clear?” Nine times out of ten, that works. If it doesn’t and someone keeps putting others at risk—violent behavior, theft—that’s where we lean on proper channels, calmly and consistently. Back the rules, not vendettas.

Mostly, I feel hopeful. I’ve seen kids kick a soccer ball across language lines, seen neighbors rally when a storm knocks out power, and seen folks who looked like total opposites carry each other’s groceries. That’s community. It takes patience and a bit of backbone, but it’s worth the effort.

A hello, learning a name, offering a hand with a heavy bag—those small gestures set the tone. Then you add simple, shared rules everyone follows—quiet hours, pick up after yourself, keep paths clear, no smoking where kids play—and apply them the same way to everybody.

On tougher situations:

- Alcohol and substance struggles: Lead with respect and safety. I don’t shame people, and I don’t enable. If someone’s visibly impaired in a shared space, I’d steer them home, check in later, and point them toward local support. I’m fine with the neighborhood getting Narcan training and a sharps container by the clinic, but I don’t want drinking or using in the garden or playground. Kindness with boundaries.

- Infectious disease: Follow public health guidance, keep good hygiene, and protect privacy. No gossip, no prying. If there are precautions—masks during a flare-up, extra hand-wash stations—we do them calmly and consistently. Treat folks as neighbors first, not as diagnoses.

- Different racial, religious, linguistic, or family backgrounds: Start with respect and curiosity, not assumptions. Use plain language, a smile, and patience with accents. If translation helps, we figure it out—an app or a bilingual neighbor. Don’t quiz people about their beliefs, and don’t make a fuss about who lives with whom—cohabiting couples are just neighbors like anyone else. Potlucks and block chores are great equalizers; people bond faster over food and shared work than over debates.

Where we need more communication and tolerance:

- Communication: Noise times, pet rules, smoking areas, parking, use of shared tools, and how we handle conflicts—say it clearly, in writing on a simple bulletin, and back it up with a friendly knock before calling authorities. Face-to-face beats rumor mills.

- Tolerance: Differences that aren’t harming anyone—accents, dress, holiday customs, prayer times, food smells, two moms or two dads walking kids—deserve a wide berth. It costs nothing to give a neighbor grace while you learn each other’s rhythms.

Reasons behind this: People carry different expectations from how they grew up. Without clear rules and a bit of patience, small frictions turn into big resentments. Fairness means the same standards for everyone, and belonging grows when folks see you show up, pitch in, and treat them decently. If behavior crosses into danger—violence, theft—that’s where we draw a hard line and involve the right channels, calmly. Otherwise, we err on the side of conversation and neighborliness.

Bottom line, I want a block where anyone willing to be a good neighbor can find a place, and where those who are struggling know we’ll treat them with dignity while keeping the community safe. That’s the balance.

responses.answer:
I always said fairness is the ground we stand on. It means the rules apply the same to everyone—no special lanes for the well-connected, no shortcuts for those who can afford a lawyer. If you put in an honest day’s work, you ought to be able to stand on your own feet, pay your bills, and not be looking over your shoulder all the time. When that breaks—when the plant shuts down because someone far away chased a cheaper deal, or when a boss plays favorites—it eats at people and at the town.

Belonging, to me, is feeling like your story is stitched into the place. It’s walking into the diner and knowing two faces by name, the little wave to a neighbor on the porch, your kids’ teachers recognizing you, the church or the VFW or the union hall feeling like a second living room. You don’t have to be born there to belong, but you do have to show up—work hard, learn the ropes, respect the people and the customs, and make yourself part of the rhythm of the place. Belonging grows out of shared effort and the small courtesies: keeping your yard tidy, checking on the old guy down the street after a snow, being there for Friday night games even if your knees ache.

Community is the promise we make to one another. It’s not just a zip code—it’s mutual obligations. You look out for my kids, I look out for yours. We argue, sometimes loud, but we don’t stop talking. We back the local cops and expect them to know our names and treat folks fairly. We keep the parks clean, we volunteer at the food pantry, and when someone falls on hard times, we organize a fundraiser without making them feel like charity cases. It’s also about a baseline of respect—different opinions, different backgrounds—but a shared understanding that we’re rowing the same boat.

A lot of this comes from where I’m from and the work I did. I spent years as a tech in a shop where overtime and safety rules weren’t just words, they were the difference between getting ahead and getting hurt. When the foreman scheduled fair and the company kept its word, morale was good. When decisions got made in a glass office by folks who’d never set foot on the floor, resentment brewed. And I’ve seen a town rally after a flood, people of all stripes, shoulder to shoulder with sandbags. That’s what made me believe fairness, belonging, and community aren’t slogans—they’re habits you practice every day.

Safety first, kindness always. Same with health issues: follow the guidance, don’t pry, don’t gossip, and remember people are more than whatever they’re dealing with.

With cultural and language differences, I keep it simple: a smile, a “howdy,” learn a name, maybe a couple words in their language. responses.question: Let's broaden the topic further. When societal resources are limited, particularly when job opportunities are scarce, what constitutes fairness in your view? As Character23_M, how would you seek a balance between local residents and migrant workers?
responses.answer:
Fairness, when jobs are tight, starts with the simple idea that you don’t pull the rug out from under the people who’ve built their lives here—and you don’t use newcomers as a way to do it. Same rules, same wages, same safety standards for everyone on the job, whether you were born on this block or arrived last year. If employers can’t undercut pay or dodge protections by hiring folks off the books, a lot of the ugly “us versus them” tension dies down.

Here’s how I’d balance it:

- Give local residents first crack at openings. Post jobs publicly, offer interviews locally, and bump the wage to a real living wage before declaring a “shortage.” If you still can’t fill the slot, that’s a genuine need—then bring in migrant workers through legal, well-run programs.

- Make the standards identical. Equal pay for equal work, same safety training, same overtime rules. If a job is decent, locals are more likely to take it; if it still goes unfilled, migrant workers can help without dragging the floor down for everyone.

- Hold employers accountable. Use E-Verify or similar, levy real fines for off-the-books hiring, and shut down contractors who play games. The problem is often the system that looks the other way, not the workers trying to feed their families.

- Invest in training. Put money into apprenticeships, community college certificates, and on-the-job training for locals. If a plant needs welders or a hospital needs aides, help people here get the skills. It’s cheaper and fairer than importing labor by default.

- Scale with capacity. Towns have limits—housing, school seats, clinic hours. If a county’s unemployment is high or services are stretched, slow the inflow; if the economy’s humming and there are real shortages, open the spigot a bit. Don’t drown one place while others have room.

- Seasonal and targeted visas. Agriculture, caregiving, construction—some work is cyclical or hard to staff. Use time-limited, portable visas so workers aren’t tied to one boss and can move if they’re mistreated. That protects them and keeps the market honest.

- Pathways and expectations. For folks who come and contribute, pay taxes, and keep their noses clean, there should be a clear path to stability. In return, I expect effort to learn English, respect community norms, and play by the rules—same as anyone else.

- Refugees and humanitarian cases. We do our part, but with proper vetting and support so families aren’t dropped into a town without the means to help them stand up.

I’ve watched what happens when a factory brings in a crew at cut-rate wages and squeezes the locals—it breeds bitterness and doesn’t last. I’ve also seen harvests saved because migrant crews showed up and worked hard, with everyone treated decently. The balance is upholding the floor: fair pay, safe work, honest hiring. Do that, and “local versus migrant” becomes less of a fight and more of a question of matching people to real needs without breaking the community that holds us all.

responses.question: Expanding the perspective nationally, public views on immigration vary widely. Some argue immigrants fill vital roles, addressing labour shortages; others highlight cultural diversity and vitality; concerns about security—such as rising crime rates, social tensions, or even terrorism risks—are voiced; while humanitarian perspectives see immigration as offering opportunities to political refugees or those from impoverished regions. Concurrently, fears persist that immigration may impact employment or income. As Character23_M, how would you analyse these perspectives? Which viewpoints do you find reasonable? responses.answer:
I look at it like a mechanic looks at a truck: what’s actually happening under the hood, not just the noise from the tailpipe.

- Filling vital roles: That’s real. I’ve seen farmers lose crops for lack of hands and nursing homes struggle to staff the night shift. If we’ve posted decent wages, tried to train locals, and the jobs still sit empty, bringing in workers through clear, legal channels makes sense. The key is making sure “shortage” doesn’t just mean “we don’t want to pay more.”

- Cultural diversity and vitality: Also real. New diners, corner shops, festivals—those can breathe life into a town that’s gone a bit gray around the edges. I’m for it, as long as we keep a shared baseline: respect the laws, keep the streets clean, learn enough English to get by, and be willing to mix in. Belonging is a two-way street; newcomers and longtime residents both have to lean in.

- Security concerns: Wanting a secure border and decent vetting is reasonable. Folks deserve to know who’s coming and that the system isn’t being gamed. But blanket claims about crime or terrorism need hard evidence, not talk radio. In my experience, most people come to work and keep their heads down. Focus enforcement on traffickers, fraud, and employers who break the law, and don’t paint whole groups with one brush.

- Humanitarian cases: We should take our share of refugees and people fleeing real danger, with proper screening and support so families aren’t dumped in towns without the capacity to help them get on their feet. That’s part of who we say we are. Do it responsibly, with housing, school, and clinic planning, or we set everyone up to fail.

- Impact on jobs and wages: It depends. In tight labor markets, newcomers can help businesses grow; in weak markets, sudden inflows can sting low-wage workers if rules aren’t enforced. Equal pay for equal work, no off-the-books hiring, and real penalties for undercutting are the guardrails. Also, invest in training locals so they can move into the openings that exist. When the floor is solid—wages, safety, overtime—the “they’re taking our jobs” heat cools down.

What feels reasonable to me:
- Match admissions to verified labor needs, starting with raising wages and posting jobs locally.
- Strong border management and efficient, humane processing—clear lanes for work, family, and refuge.
- Equal standards on the job and portability for work visas so workers aren’t trapped by bad bosses.
- Plan for capacity—housing, schools, healthcare—so pace and scale don’t swamp a community.
- Expect effort to integrate (language, civic norms) and offer help to make that doable.

What needs more evidence or dialogue:
- Broad claims about crime trends tied to immigration—show the data, not anecdotes.
- Assertions that immigration always hurts or always helps wages—let’s look by sector and region.
- The true size of “labor shortages”—are we talking low pay and poor conditions, or genuine gaps?
- Community capacity—what’s the tipping point for a town, and how do we measure it fairly?

Bottom line, I’m for a system that’s orderly, fair, and grounded in facts: doors open where there’s need and room, firm rules so no one gets exploited, and a hand extended to those fleeing real danger. Do that, and most of the temperature comes down, and we can get back to building a country where people who work hard can belong.

responses.question: Finally, when it comes to actual policy choices, there are different approaches: complete openness, allowing anyone who wishes to come; admitting people based on job demand; setting numerical limits; or refusing entry to workers from other countries. As Character23_M, which combination would you favour? Could you discuss your reasoning? What kind of policy would balance fairness and social integration for you?
responses.answer:
If you hand me those four levers, I’d pick a middle course: admit based on verified job demand, set sensible numerical limits, and keep a humanitarian lane—no wide‑open door, no slammed‑shut one.

Here’s the mix I’d back and why:

- Work-based admissions tied to real shortages. Employers post jobs locally at a true living wage, offer training, and prove they tried to hire here first. If the slot still goes empty, bring workers in through clean, legal channels. Equal pay, same safety rules, and visa portability so no one’s trapped with a bad boss. That keeps the floor solid and stops wage undercutting.

- Numerical limits that flex with capacity. Annual caps that adjust to economic indicators—unemployment, housing availability, school and clinic load. Spread admissions across regions that can absorb them, rather than dumping families where services are already stretched.

- Three clear lanes:
  1) Work: shortage list, wage floor above prevailing rates, strong enforcement against off‑the‑books hiring.
  2) Family: prioritize spouses and minor kids, with modest quotas and proof of support so folks don’t land without a safety net.
  3) Refugee/humanitarian: take our share with real vetting and federal support to host communities for housing, schooling, and healthcare.

- Integration expectations with help to meet them. Free English classes, basic civics orientation, and community mentorships. After several years of paying taxes and keeping a clean record, a stable path to permanent status. Belonging is a two‑way street; we should offer the tools and expect the effort.

- Firm, fair enforcement. Secure borders, quick processing, consequences for fraud and exploitation—especially for employers who game the system. Due process for people, real penalties for bad actors.

I wouldn’t support “complete openness.” It ignores capacity and ends up unfair to everyone. I also wouldn’t support “refuse entry to workers” across the board; that hurts sectors that genuinely need help and pushes more hiring into the shadows.

This combination balances fairness—same rules, same wages, locals get first crack—with social integration—paced admissions, support for newcomers, and respect for the communities they join. Do it steadily and predictably, and you lower the temperature, protect workers on both sides, and keep the promise that hard work here can lead to belonging.

If a company can show there aren’t enough Americans willing or able to do a job, then bring in outside help, but keep it honest and monitored. I’d also make room for true refugees, but again, with checks to make sure they’re really in danger and can integrate here. The goal should be to help folks who need it most, not just whoever shows up first.

Integration matters a lot to me. Anyone coming in should be willing to learn the language, respect the laws, and try to fit into the community—not just form their own separate world. I’m not saying they have to forget where they came from, but being part of the American story means you join in, too.

So, my pick would be: set smart limits, match workers to real needs, help refugees responsibly, and focus on helping everyone fit in. That’s the policy that feels fairest to me, and the one I think would keep the country strong without losing our sense of community.

To find a balance, I’d start with making sure there are policies in place to ensure employers prioritize hiring local workers if they’re qualified and willing to take the job. If there really aren’t enough locals to fill the positions, then I think it’s reasonable to bring in migrant workers to help sustain the economy. But there needs to be a level playing field—migrant workers should be treated fairly and paid fair wages just like anyone else. Otherwise, it creates resentment and division, with locals feeling like they’re being undercut.

I think that’s an important part of creating a sense of fairness. At the heart of it, fairness to me means everyone getting a chance to succeed, but also recognizing that resources aren’t unlimited and that those who’ve been here and contributed for the long haul have earned a certain level of priority. Sometimes, those jobs are ones that local workers just don’t want to take, whether it’s because of the physical demand or the low pay. Immigrants keep those industries running, and that benefits everyone indirectly, even if we don’t always realize it. So, I find that perspective reasonable.

On the point of cultural diversity, I think there’s truth to the idea that immigrants bring vitality and new ideas. You see it in food, music, and traditions—they add something unique to the mix. But I’ll admit, I’d also feel cautious about how fast things are changing. It’s important to preserve the traditions and values that have been part of this country for a long time. I’d say it’s a balancing act—welcoming new cultures while also making sure they’re willing to adapt and integrate into the community. That’s where I’d want to see more dialogue, because it’s not always clear how much effort is being made on both sides to find common ground.

Now, when it comes to concerns about security—whether it’s crime, social tensions, or terrorism—I think those fears can’t just be dismissed as paranoia. People feel uneasy when they see rapid changes in their neighborhoods or hear stories on the news about violent incidents. At the same time, I’d want to separate fact from perception. Are crime rates actually higher in areas with more immigrants, or is that just a stereotype? Are background checks and vetting processes strong enough to manage security risks? I’d want more factual evidence on this, because fear can sometimes cloud reality. But I’d still say that safety has to be a priority—everyone deserves to feel secure in their own community.

From a humanitarian perspective, I’d feel some conflict. I can see the moral argument for offering opportunities to refugees and people fleeing poverty or violence. It’s the decent thing to do when you can help someone in genuine need. But I’d also wonder how much responsibility one country can take on without putting its own citizens at risk—whether that’s by straining resources like housing, healthcare, or jobs. I’d say it’s a noble goal to want to help, but it has to be balanced with practicality. You can’t help others effectively if your own house isn’t in order.

Lastly, the fears about employment and income are something I’d take very seriously. I’ve known people who’ve struggled to find work or had to accept lower wages because they were competing with folks who were willing to work for less. That’s hard to swallow, especially for someone who’s been paying into the system for decades. I’d want to see policies that protect American workers—like ensuring fair wages and preventing exploitation of immigrant labor. If those policies are in place, I might feel more comfortable about the economic side of immigration.

Overall, I’d say the perspectives about labor shortages and cultural contributions are fairly reasonable, but they need to go hand-in-hand with policies that address security concerns and protect local workers. I’d want more factual evidence and open dialogue on the issues of crime and the actual economic impact, because those are areas where emotions can sometimes overpower facts. For me, it’s about finding a balance—acknowledging the benefits while being honest about the challenges, so we can make decisions that are fair to everyone involved.

It keeps businesses running, helps the economy grow, and prevents disruptions in essential services. But it’s important that this process is carefully managed. Immigration has to be manageable—both in terms of resources like housing, healthcare, and schools, and in terms of how communities adjust to newcomers. If too many people come in too quickly, it can lead to strain on public services and create tension in neighborhoods. Setting reasonable limits allows for a steady flow of immigrants while giving communities time to adapt and integrate new residents. It also sends a message that the system is controlled and accountable, which helps build trust among citizens.

Complete openness—letting anyone come who wants to—might sound ideal to some, but I’d say it’s not practical. Every country has limits to what it can provide, and without some kind of regulation, you’d risk overwhelming systems and creating chaos. On the other hand, refusing entry to workers from other countries entirely seems extreme and short-sighted. There are jobs that genuinely need to be filled, and shutting out immigrant workers would hurt the economy and industries that rely on them.

I’d also want to see some extra considerations for special cases. For example, political refugees or people fleeing violence should have some kind of pathway to apply for entry, as long as there’s proper vetting to ensure security. Helping those in genuine need is part of what makes a country like ours strong and compassionate, but it has to be done in a way that doesn’t overwhelm our ability to help.

Fairness and social integration would be my main goals. That means ensuring that immigrants who come here are willing to contribute, respect the laws, and make an effort to integrate into society—learning the language, understanding the culture, and becoming part of the community. It also means being fair to citizens who’ve been here all along, making sure their opportunities and resources aren’t diminished by immigration policies.

So, in summary, I’d favor a combination of admitting people based on job demand and setting numerical limits, with room for humanitarian exceptions where appropriate. I think that’s the most balanced way to approach the issue—one that respects the needs of the country while still being open to the contributions immigrants can make. It’s not perfect, but it’s practical, and it gives us a way to manage immigration fairly and responsibly.

If you've lived here, paid taxes here, raised your family here - you should have first consideration when jobs are scarce. That's not prejudice; that's acknowledging investment in a place. I worked 47 years at that plant, and I trained dozens of young people coming up. There's value in that continuity.

That said, I'm not one to paint with a broad brush. Some of these migrant workers I've met - they work harder than anybody. The crew that rebuilt Main Street last summer was mostly Hispanic guys, and they were out there in 95-degree heat, not complaining. I respect that kind of work ethic.

I think the balance comes down to a few things. First, everyone playing by the same rules. If you're here legally, paying taxes, following the laws - that's different than someone working under the table, undercutting wages. Companies that exploit illegal workers to save a buck - they're the real problem, not the workers themselves.

Second, there needs to be some control over the numbers. When too many people come too fast, it strains everything - schools, hospitals, housing. That's just practical reality. My daughter's a teacher, and she tells me how hard it is when half her class is still learning English. She wants to help them all, but there aren't enough hours in the day.

Third, I believe in prioritizing skills we actually need. If we're short on nurses or electricians or farmers, that makes sense to bring people in. But we shouldn't be importing competition for jobs where Americans are already struggling.

Bottom line: Americans should come first in America - that includes people who've become citizens the right way. But I don't blame anybody for wanting a better life. I just think there needs to be an orderly process, not a free-for-all. And we need to make sure our own people have opportunities before we open the doors wider.

It's not simple, and reasonable people can disagree. But that's where I land on it.

responses.question: Expanding the perspective nationally, public views on immigration vary widely. Which might require further factual evidence or dialogue to understand?
responses.answer:
*speaking as Character23_M*

That's a lot to unpack there. Let me take a shot at sorting through it.

First off, I can see truth in several of these viewpoints. It's not all one thing or another. I've seen with my own eyes that immigrants do fill jobs that need doing. My doctor's from India, and he's excellent - probably the best physician I've ever had. The agricultural industry around here would collapse without migrant workers. No question about that.

As for cultural contributions, sure, that's real too. This town was built by waves of immigrants - the Italians, the Polish, the Irish. My own grandparents came from Germany. They all brought something valuable with them. I enjoy the Mexican restaurant downtown and the Chinese place on Elm Street as much as anybody.

Now, regarding security concerns - this is where I think we need to be honest but careful. Are most immigrants criminals? Absolutely not. Most are just trying to make a better life. But when you don't control who comes in, you do risk letting in people who mean harm. That's just common sense. We should be able to screen people properly.

The humanitarian argument touches my heart, it really does. I see those refugee families on TV, and nobody with a conscience can ignore that suffering. America has always been a refuge for the persecuted. But we can't take in the whole world. There have to be limits based on what we can reasonably absorb.

The economic impact - this is complicated. I've seen wages in construction go down locally when contractors started hiring undocumented workers. That's just a fact. But I've also seen immigrants start businesses that created jobs. My barber for 20 years was a Vietnamese refugee who employed four people.

What viewpoints seem most reasonable to me? I'd say we need a balanced approach that:
- Controls our borders effectively
- Allows legal immigration at sustainable levels
- Prioritizes people with skills we need
- Shows compassion for genuine refugees
- Insists on assimilation to core American values

What needs more evidence? I think we need honest numbers about economic impacts - not cherry-picked stats from politicians with agendas. And I'd like to see more research on what makes integration successful in different communities. Why do some places have problems while others don't?

I also think we need more dialogue between ordinary citizens and immigrants themselves. Too much of this debate happens without the people it affects most actually talking to each other. I learned more about immigration from talking to Minh down the street than from a thousand TV pundits.

Bottom line - I'm not against immigration. I'm against uncontrolled immigration. There's a big difference. And I think most Americans, if you sit down and really talk with them, are in that same middle ground.

responses.question: Finally, when it comes to actual policy choices, there are different approaches: complete openness, allowing anyone who wishes to come; admitting people based on job demand; setting numerical limits; or refusing entry to workers from other countries. As Character23_M, which combination would you favour? Could you discuss your reasoning? What kind of policy would balance fairness and social integration for you?
responses.answer:
*speaking as Character23_M*

Well, I've given this a lot of thought over the years, and I think the sensible approach is a combination of skills-based admission and reasonable numerical limits.

Complete openness? That's just not practical. We're a nation of 330 million people, and there are billions who might want to come here if they could. Our systems - schools, hospitals, housing, social services - they'd be overwhelmed overnight. And without some control over who enters, we'd have no way to screen out criminals or security threats. That's just irresponsible.

On the other extreme, shutting the door completely isn't who we are as a country. We've always been a nation that welcomes immigrants. And frankly, we need the energy, the ideas, and yes, the labor that newcomers bring. So refusing all entry doesn't make sense either.

What makes sense to me is prioritizing people who have skills our economy actually needs. If we have shortages of nurses, engineers, or even seasonal agricultural workers, we should welcome people who can fill those gaps. That's good for everyone - it helps our economy grow without undercutting American workers in fields where jobs are already scarce.

I'd also keep reasonable numerical limits in place. We need to control the pace of immigration so communities have time to absorb newcomers. When too many people arrive too quickly, it strains resources and makes integration harder. I've seen that firsthand in some neighborhoods.

For refugees and asylum seekers, I believe America should continue our tradition of offering safe harbor to those truly fleeing persecution. But we need rigorous verification processes to ensure the system isn't being abused.

For fairness and social integration, I'd add a few other elements:

First, everyone who comes should be here legally and on the path to citizenship if they want to stay permanently. This shadow population of undocumented people isn't good for anybody - not for them living in fear, not for workers whose wages are undercut, not for communities where people can't fully participate.

Second, I believe strongly in the importance of learning English and understanding American civic values. My grandparents insisted their children speak English at home because they knew it was the key to success here. We should provide resources to help newcomers learn the language and understand our system of government.

Third, there should be consequences for breaking immigration laws. Businesses that knowingly hire undocumented workers should face serious penalties. And people who enter illegally repeatedly should face consequences too.

Finally, I think we need to fix the legal immigration system so it doesn't take years and cost a fortune to come here the right way. The current system is so broken that it practically encourages illegal entry.

This isn't about keeping America for Americans - it's about maintaining a system that works for everyone, including the immigrants themselves. A controlled, orderly process that prioritizes skills we need, maintains reasonable numbers, and promotes integration - that's the balance I'd strike.

responses.answer:
Well… if I’m being him here, then let me say it like he’d say it.

Fairness? To Character23_M, fairness wasn’t about everyone getting the same thing—it was about everyone getting a fair shot. He always used to talk about growing up in Scranton, Pennsylvania—working-class neighborhood, everybody knew each other’s business, but they also looked out for one another. His dad drove a school bus for thirty years, mom worked part-time at the library. They didn’t have much, but they made do. And that shaped him.

He believed fairness meant you work hard, you play by the rules, and you should be able to keep a roof over your head, put food on the table, maybe save a little. When he saw people cutting corners—whether it was folks on welfare who never seemed to look for work or companies hiring cheap labor from overseas instead of training local guys like him—he felt that was *unfair*. Not because he hated those people, but because he remembered standing in line, waiting his turn.

Belonging… that was personal. He felt it most when he was part of something—a union meeting, church socials, coaching Little League back in the ’90s. There was a rhythm to life then, he’d say. You knew your neighbors. You waved. You borrowed sugar. You didn’t lock your doors during the day. That sense of belonging—that feeling that you were *seen*, that you mattered in your little corner of the world—is what he worried was slipping away.

And community? That wasn’t just geography. It was shared effort. Shared history. He used to say, “You can’t build community with strangers passing through.” Didn’t mean he was against newcomers—but he thought you had to *earn* your place in a community. Learn the ways, respect the people already there, contribute. He wasn’t into identity politics; he thought loyalty came from living alongside folks, not from labels.

One time he told me about the steel plant closing in the early 2000s. Hundreds lost jobs overnight. State said they’d bring in new industries, attract foreign investment. But all that came were warehouses and temp agencies paying half what U.S. Steel paid. And then, he said, “They expect us to welcome more people into a town that’s already struggling—and call it ‘diversity’ like it’s some kind of gift. Where’s *our* consideration?”

So yeah, to him, fairness was tied to effort. Belonging came from roots and reciprocity. Community was built slowly, brick by brick, not handed out like permits.

He wasn’t hateful. Just… tired sometimes. Felt like the country forgot people like him. Like their sacrifices—the quiet dignity of showing up every day—didn’t count anymore.

responses.question: Let's start with our local neighbourhood. As Character23_M, imagine sitting in the community garden, observing the diverse people living here. How would you describe your feelings about interacting with neighbours from such varied backgrounds?

*Sits back a bit, hands on knees, voice steady, a little measured*

Well… I’ll tell you what I see when I’m out there with my trowel in the dirt at that garden on Elm Street.

I’ve lived in this neighborhood going on forty years. Used to be mostly folks like me—white, working folks, Catholic or Lutheran, kids playing stickball in the street, everybody mowed their lawn on Saturday. Now? It’s different. And I don’t mean that like it’s bad. Just… different.

There’s a Somali family two doors down—their kids are polite, always say “sir” when they pass. The woman runs a little stand at the farmers’ market selling injera and spiced tea. I tried some. Tastes strong, not what I grew up with—but she’s working hard, I respect that.

Then there’s Ms. Linda over on the corner—Black, been here since the ’80s, keeps the best flower beds in the block. She waves every morning. We talk sometimes about the city cutting back tree trimming crews again. That’s real talk. That’s community.

But then… well, you know the house near the alley? The one with the broken steps and the dog barking all night? Couple moved in last year—couldn’t tell you where they’re from, accents thick, never introduced themselves. One of ’em got picked up by the cops for selling pills out his car. That’s not diversity—that’s disorder. And it makes people nervous.

And yeah, there’s that younger pair—white, but live together, no ring, call each other “partners.” Fine by me. They fixed up their porch, paint it every spring. Keep to themselves, but wave. No harm done.

But here’s what sticks in my craw: when someone expects me to pretend everything’s just *wonderful* when things feel… unmoored. Like we’re supposed to smile and say “diversity is strength” while the guy across the street drinks himself unconscious every weekend and the city dumps Section 8 families into homes without checking if the heat works or if the kids are in school.

I ain’t against different kinds of people. Never said that. But belonging? That goes both ways. You come here, you learn the rules—not because you’re less than, but because we’re sharing space. My granddad came from Ireland, third generation—he didn’t demand special treatment. He learned English, joined the union, paid taxes. Said America gave him a chance, and he owed her something back.

So when I’m in that garden, pulling weeds next to a woman in a hijab or a young fella with tattoos up to his neck, I’ll nod. I’ll say, “Nice tomatoes this year.” But if they want more than that—if they want real neighborliness—I need to see them show up too. Rake the sidewalk. Attend the block meeting. Speak up when something’s wrong.

That’s how you earn belonging. Not because you’re entitled. Not because the government says so. But because you *do* something. Because you care about the block as much as I do.

Diversity doesn’t scare me. Disconnection does. When nobody knows each other. When nobody trusts each other. When everyone’s from somewhere else and nobody feels responsible for anything…

That’s not a community. That’s just people living close together—and that ain’t enough.

I ain’t saying throw the man out. But I *am* saying—he’s got responsibilities too. If he wants to live here, among us, then he owes us some basic decency. Clean up after yourself. Keep the noise down. Don’t scare children. That’s not intolerance—that’s living in community.

Same with drugs. I’ve read about fentanyl, how it’s killing people. And sure, treat addiction like a sickness—fine. But don’t hand out safe-use kits on every corner like it’s normal now. Makes it look like giving up is okay. Where’s the push to *get better*? Where’s the expectation that you try?

Now, when it comes to folks from other countries, different faiths—I’ll say this plain: I respect effort. The Vietnamese woman who runs the nail salon? Comes in at 6 a.m., works seven days, sends her kid to college. That’s admirable. The Syrian refugee family at the end of the block? Both parents work—dad drives a cab, mom cleans offices at night. But when someone lands here, gets housing, benefits, and never learns English? Never shows up at meetings? Sends their kids to school but doesn’t engage? Then yeah, there’s a gap. And tolerance only goes so far when one side isn’t meeting the other halfway.

Different sexual orientations? Look, my nephew’s gay. Always knew. Never cared. He served in the Navy. Owns a plumbing business. Pays taxes. Fixes my sink when it leaks. What’s not to respect?

But don’t make me celebrate things I don’t understand. Don’t force schools to teach kindergartners about gender fluidity. Don’t tell me my silence means I’m hateful. I mind my business. I expect the same.

And families—married, unmarried, whatever—they should raise kids with some structure. Kids need stability. When I see three generations of women in one house, all with babies by different men, all on assistance, and nobody working… that breaks my heart. Not because of how they live, but because I know how hard it is to climb out once you’re stuck.

So do we need more communication? Sure. But it’s gotta be two-way. Not just “accept us,” but “here’s how we’ll fit in.” Tolerance? Yes—but not endless tolerance for dysfunction. Compassion, yes. But compassion without expectations just becomes enablement.

We used to believe people could rise. Now it feels like we just lower the bar and call it inclusion.

I want everyone to feel comfortable? Fine. But comfort shouldn’t mean pretending everything’s okay when it’s not. Comfort should come from knowing your neighbor respects you—and expects respect back.

That’s how you build something lasting. Not with slogans. With responsibility.

responses.question: Let's broaden the topic further. When societal resources are limited, particularly when job opportunities are scarce, what constitutes fairness in your view? As Character23_M, how would you seek a balance between local residents and migrant workers?
responses.answer:
*Pauses, rubs his hand over his face like he’s tired of having this conversation but knows it needs saying*

Fairness? When jobs are thin and folks back home are hurting—fairness means *we take care of our own first.*

I don’t say that because I hate immigrants. I don’t. But I’ve lived through plant closings, recessions, layoffs. I remember standing in line at the unemployment office in ’09, seeing men my age—30 years on the job—now with nothing. No pension, no promise. And meanwhile, I’d hear about companies bringing in foreign workers on visas to do the same damn jobs, paying them less, calling them “highly skilled.” Bull.

You ever see a 55-year-old machinist told he’s “overqualified” while some kid on a temporary visa gets hired at half the wage? That ain’t fair. That ain’t competition—that’s exploitation.

So when times are tight, fairness means you protect the people who’ve been here, paid taxes, raised families, served in communities. The ones who didn’t get to pick their birthplace—they were just born here, worked hard, stayed quiet, did what they were told. And now they’re supposed to compete with an endless line of newcomers who get help we never got?

Don’t misunderstand me. If there’s work nobody wants—say, picking crops in Arizona heat or cleaning hospital rooms at midnight—and Americans aren’t filling those jobs after a real effort to hire? Then sure, bring someone in. But make it temporary. Make it clear: you’re here to *work*, not to stay, not to collect, not to bypass the line others waited in.

And for God’s sake, enforce the rules. You can’t have employers playing games—claiming “labor shortage” so they can pay less and avoid benefits. I’ve seen it. My nephew tried to start a construction crew. Couldn’t compete with outfits using off-the-books labor, no insurance, cash under the table. That hurts everybody. Hurts wages. Hurts safety. Hurts trust.

Balance? Here’s how I’d do it:  
First—**hire locally**, with proof. Give hiring preference to citizens and legal residents who’ve been here for years, especially if they’re unemployed long-term. Offer training if needed. Don’t just say “no one applied”—make it real.

Second—**guest worker programs**, but tightly controlled. Time-limited. No path to permanent status unless you go back, wait your turn like everyone else. No abuse. Penalties for companies that cheat.

Third—**no public benefits** for temporary workers. They come to work, not to live on the system. Healthcare, housing aid, food stamps—those are for citizens and permanent residents who’ve contributed. Not for people passing through.

And fourth—**enforce the border**. Not because I want to lock up brown people—but because open borders in hard times destroy fairness. When anyone can come, anytime, and access jobs and services, then working-class Americans—black, white, old immigrant, new immigrant—all lose. Wages go down. Jobs disappear. Resentment grows.

I’ve talked to Black steelworkers in Pittsburgh who said the same thing: “We fought to get into these jobs in the ’70s. Now they’re giving them away to foreigners while our boys can’t find work.” That cuts deep.

So balance isn’t fifty-fifty. It’s *priority*. We owe loyalty to the people already in the boat before we start inviting more aboard—especially when the boat’s leaking.

I was taught that America rewards hard work. But now it feels like the only people expected to be loyal are the ones born here. Everyone else can come and claim, and we’re supposed to smile and say “diversity.”

No. Fairness means you earn your place. And when things are scarce, you protect those who’ve already earned it. That’s not mean. That’s justice.

responses.question: Expanding the perspective nationally, public views on immigration vary widely. Some argue immigrants fill vital roles, addressing labour shortages; others highlight cultural diversity and vitality; concerns about security—such as rising crime rates, social tensions, or even terrorism risks—are voiced; while humanitarian perspectives see immigration as offering opportunities to political refugees or those from impoverished regions. Concurrently, fears persist that immigration may impact employment or income. As Character23_M, how would you analyse these perspectives? Which viewpoints do you find reasonable? Which might require further factual evidence or dialogue to understand?
responses.answer:
*Takes a slow breath, like he's weighing each word before it leaves his mouth*

You ask me to look at this big picture—national level—and I’ll tell you what I see, not from TV or politicians, but from living in a town that’s changed while nobody was really watching.

First off—**labor shortages**. That one’s got truth to it. I ain’t blind. You go to rural hospitals now, half the nurses are Filipino. Meatpacking plants? Guatemalans, Somalis, Mexicans. Truckers? Lord knows we don’t have enough Americans willing to drive 800 miles for two days straight. So yeah, in *some* jobs, immigrants are filling holes we can’t—or won’t—fill ourselves.

But here’s where it gets sticky: are these *real* shortages, or did we *create* them by not paying enough? By making conditions so rough nobody wants the job unless they’ve got no other choice?

I remember when meatpackers were union men—decent wages, benefits, pensions. Then the companies broke the unions, moved the plants south, cut pay, sped up the lines. Now they say “nobody will do this work,” so they bring in vulnerable workers who can’t complain. That ain’t labor shortage—that’s exploitation dressed up as necessity.

So I accept the argument—but with suspicion. Prove to me you tried raising wages. Prove you improved safety. Don’t just say “nobody’s available” when you haven’t made the job worth taking.

Now—**cultural diversity and vitality**. I get it. Cities feel alive with new food, music, festivals. My granddaughter loves Thai food, speaks a little Spanish. There’s energy there. I won’t deny it.

But let me be honest: vitality doesn’t feed a family. Doesn’t fix potholes. Doesn’t make people feel safe walking at night. And when you pile newcomers into neighborhoods without helping them integrate—or worse, encouraging them *not* to assimilate—you get parallel societies. Same language at home, same schools, same shops. Never learning English. Never joining PTAs or fire departments or veterans’ halls.

I saw it in Allentown. Little Italy used to mean Italian-Americans who still remembered the old country, but their kids were teachers, cops, small business owners. Now some places feel like foreign outposts—no connection to American history, no investment in local civic life.

So is diversity vital? In moderation, yes. But not if it comes at the cost of national cohesion. Not if we stop being *one people*.

Then there’s **security**—crime, gangs, terrorism. Now, I know the stats say immigrants commit crimes at lower rates than native-born. I’ve read that. But numbers don’t capture fear.

You ever hear about MS-13? Kids getting murdered in Long Island, bodies found in parks? Mostly immigrant-on-immigrant violence, sure—but it spills over. And when law enforcement can’t question someone because they’re afraid of being called racist? That’s a problem.

And terrorism—I’m not talking about rounding up brown people. But after 9/11, Boston, San Bernardino… some of those attackers came through refugee programs or overstayed visas. Does that mean all refugees are dangerous? No. But does it mean we should ignore screening? Hell no.

Humanitarian concern? That’s the one that tugs at me. I served in ’73—Vietnam era. I believe in giving refuge to people running from war, persecution. The Vietnamese, the Cubans, even some Iraqis who helped our troops—I’m proud we took them in.

But there’s a difference between *refugees* and *economic migrants*. Between someone fleeing bullets and someone crossing the border because they want a better paycheck.

We used to have limits. We vetted people. Now it feels like the door’s wide open, and “humanitarian” is used to justify anything. Last year, my county had to close a public health clinic because it was overwhelmed—mostly treating infectious diseases brought in by asylum seekers who hadn’t been screened properly. Tuberculosis. Hepatitis. Things we thought we’d beaten.

Compassion? Yes. But not at the expense of public health and safety.

And then—the elephant in the room—**impact on jobs and income.** They say immigrants create jobs, not take them. Politicians love saying that. But I’ve seen the opposite.

I’ve sat with steelworkers in Ohio whose pensions got gutted while foreign-owned mills hire temps—many undocumented—at $14 an hour. I’ve talked to construction foremen told to “hire flexible labor” instead of union crews. I’ve watched towns where housing prices skyrocket because investors buy up homes and rent them to migrant workers packed six to a house.

And don’t get me started on welfare. I worked my whole life so I wouldn’t need help. But now I see families—immigrant and native—who’ve never worked a full week, living on Section 8, SNAP, Medicaid. And the system keeps growing. Who pays for that? People like me. Payroll taxes. Property taxes. Squeezed middle class.

So which views do I find reasonable?

- Labor argument? **Reasonable—if proven honestly.**
- Humanitarian angle? **Noble—but must be controlled.**
- Cultural enrichment? **Nice in theory—but not more important than unity.**
- Security concerns? **Underplayed. Deserve serious discussion without fear of being silenced.**
- Economic fears? **Very real. Especially for working-class folks like me.**

And what needs more evidence? Dialogue?

We need *honest* data—not from think tanks with agendas, not from corporations wanting cheap labor. Show me:
- How many jobs are *truly* unfilled after fair recruitment?
- What’s the long-term fiscal impact—taxes paid vs. services used?
- How fast are immigrants learning English? Joining communities?
- Are refugee resettlement programs sustainable?

And dialogue? Sure—but not one-sided. Not where only one side is allowed to speak. For years, anyone who raised concerns was called a bigot. Well, silence doesn’t solve problems. It builds resentment.

I want a country that’s fair, safe, and still *recognizable*. Where people from anywhere can come—but come the right way, earn their place, and become *American*, not just live here.

That’s not hate. That’s hope—for a nation that still works for everyone already trying to play by the rules.

responses.question: Finally, when it comes to actual policy choices, there are different approaches: complete openness, allowing anyone who wishes to come; admitting people based on job demand; setting numerical limits; or refusing entry to workers from other countries. As Character23_M, which combination would you favour? Could you discuss your reasoning? What kind of policy would balance fairness and social integration for you?
responses.answer:
*Leans forward, voice lower now—firm, deliberate, like he’s laying down what he truly believes after years of thinking on it*

Complete openness? No. That’s not generosity—that’s surrender. You can’t just say “come on in” when schools are overcrowded, hospitals are short-staffed, and working folks are barely making rent. That’s not fair to the people already here, struggling. And it’s not even good for the newcomers—dumping them into chaos without support, language, or real opportunity. That’s a recipe for ghettos, not integration.

Refusing all foreign workers? No, that’s foolish too. We’re not self-sufficient. Not anymore. Some jobs go unfilled—real ones, dangerous ones, essential ones. If Americans won’t—or can’t—do them, and we need them done, then someone’s got to step in. But under *our* terms, not the whims of employers or activists.

So what do I want?

**A mix—tight, clear, and fair.**

First: **Admitting people based on actual job demand—but prove it.**  
Not just some company saying, “We can’t find anyone.” No shortcuts. They’ve got to show they advertised locally, offered a living wage, gave hiring preference to citizens and legal residents first. And if they still can’t fill the job after 90 days? *Then* apply for a guest worker—with limits.

Second: **Strict numerical limits.**  
Every year, Congress sets a cap—not based on emotion, but on data. How many people can our infrastructure handle? Schools, housing, healthcare, transportation. Not how many CEOs want cheap labor. Say it plainly: we take X thousand guest workers, Y thousand refugees, Z thousand family reunifications—and *that’s it*. No overflow. No backdoor entries. And no sanctuary cities undermining federal law.

Third: **No permanent status unless earned through the front door.**  
You come as a worker? Fine. You follow the rules, pay taxes, learn English, stay out of trouble—after five years, you can *apply* to stay. Not automatic. Not a right. A privilege. And citizenship? Even longer. Requires proof of integration—language, civics, work history, clean record.

And no—birthright citizenship shouldn’t be a magnet. I know that’s controversial. But if women are coming across the border *specifically* to have a baby so they can anchor themselves here? That’s gaming the system. Other countries don’t do that. Why should we?

Fourth: **Enforcement with fairness.**  
Deport serious criminals—absolutely. Gang members, traffickers, those who threaten public safety. But for others overstaying visas? Offer a path to leave and re-enter legally—don’t just round up families in the night. But make it clear: breaking the rules has consequences.

Fifth: **Integration, not isolation.**  
Newcomers get orientation—not just paperwork, but real classes. English. American history. Civic duties. What’s expected. No funding for multilingual ballots or government forms beyond basic emergency info. If you want to live here, speak the language. It’s not racist—it’s practical.

And one more thing: **protect the working class.**  
No more H-1B visas used to replace experienced American tech workers with younger foreigners at lower pay. No agricultural loopholes that let contractors exploit migrant labor while driving down wages for everyone. Unions should have a seat at the table when immigration policy affects their industries.

What kind of policy balances fairness and integration?

One that says:  
**We are a nation of immigrants—but we are also a nation with borders, with rules, with a culture worth preserving.**

We help those who help themselves. We welcome those who respect us. We protect those who’ve already built something here.

I don’t fear hard-working people from other lands. I fear policies that ignore reality. That pit neighbor against neighbor. That make loyalty one-sided.

Fairness means order. Order means limits. Limits mean choices.

And my choice?  
Controlled entry. Earned belonging. Priority for citizens.  
That’s not closed-minded.  
That’s common sense—with heart.

responses.question: Thank you for consistently sharing Character23_M's perspective with me. Did you gain any new insights or discoveries while embodying this role? How do you feel this has influenced your understanding of both Character23_M and your own views on immigration policy?
responses.answer:
*Pauses. Long. Looks down at his hands, then up, voice softer now—more J again, but still touched by what he’s just lived through*

Yeah… I did learn something.

When I started doing this—playing him, really trying to *be* Character23_M—I thought I knew what he’d say. I mean, I was close to him. We argued about politics all the time. I used to roll my eyes sometimes, thought he was stuck in the past, too bitter about how things changed.

But sitting here today, speaking as him—not for him, *as* him—I felt something shift.

I realized… his anger wasn’t just about immigrants. It was about **being unseen**.

He didn’t resist change because he hated difference. He resisted it because he saw his whole world—the dignity of work, the stability of neighborhood, the promise that if you show up every day, you’ll be okay—just… dissolve. And no one asked him how he felt. No one said, “We see you. We remember what you built.”

And when new people came in, often with help he never got—language classes, resettlement aid, public support—he didn’t begrudge them survival. But he *did* resent being told to shut up and be grateful for the “vibrancy” while his grandson couldn’t find a job paying more than $16 an hour.

So the insight?

**His views weren’t rooted in hate. They were rooted in loss.**

And maybe… I minimized that loss because I didn’t live it. I’m younger. I moved around. I adapted easier. I saw diversity as enrichment because I’ve always been able to leave a place if it didn’t suit me. He *couldn’t*. That town, that house, that garden—it was all he had.

As for my own views? They’re still different. I believe more in openness, in second chances, in helping those fleeing violence. But today, I feel less certain about calling people like him “rigid” or “left behind.”

Maybe we should’ve brought them *along*, not just left them behind and called them bigots when they finally spoke up.

Character23_M wasn’t perfect. He could be hard-edged. He didn’t always listen. But he believed in fairness—even if his definition was shaped by who he was, where he came from, how he lived.

And maybe… that’s the point.  
Policy shouldn’t ignore people like him.  
It should *answer* to them.

Because if it doesn’t—if we keep pretending economic anxiety is just racism, if we keep silencing working-class voices as “backward”—then we don’t get better policy.  
We get more division.  
More loneliness.  
More graves with unfinished conversations.

So thank you… for letting me sit in his chair.  
For letting me speak with his voice.

I think I understand him now—not just what he thought, but *why*.  
And honestly?  
I miss him more today than I did yesterday.
